claim: Class IV neurons in Drosophila larvae are polymodal nociceptors responsible for thermal, mechanical, and light sensation.
source: Class IV neurons in Drosophila larvae are polymodal nociceptors responsible for thermal, mechanical, and light sensation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Noxious thermal stimuli caused pauses after high-frequency spike trains in Class IV neurons.
source: We found that noxious thermal stimuli, but not blue light stimulation, caused a unique pattern of Class IV, which were composed of pauses after high-frequency spike trains and a large Ca2+ rise in the dendrite (the Ca2+ transient).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings shown in figures.

claim: Noxious thermal stimuli caused a large Ca2+ rise in the dendrite (the Ca2+ transient) in Class IV neurons.
source: We found that noxious thermal stimuli, but not blue light stimulation, caused a unique pattern of Class IV, which were composed of pauses after high-frequency spike trains and a large Ca2+ rise in the dendrite (the Ca2+ transient).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in figures.

claim: Blue light stimulation did not cause the unique firing pattern with pauses after high-frequency spike trains in Class IV neurons.
source: We found that noxious thermal stimuli, but not blue light stimulation, caused a unique pattern of Class IV, which were composed of pauses after high-frequency spike trains and a large Ca2+ rise in the dendrite (the Ca2+ transient).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings comparing thermal and light stimuli.

claim: Both the unique firing pattern and the Ca2+ transient depend on two TRPA channels.
source: Both these responses depended on two TRPA channels and the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel (L-VGCC), showing that the thermosensation provokes Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic experiments using mutants of dTrpA1 and painless genes.

claim: Both the unique firing pattern and the Ca2+ transient depend on the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel (L-VGCC).
source: Both these responses depended on two TRPA channels and the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel (L-VGCC), showing that the thermosensation provokes Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic experiments using Ca-α1D mutants and pharmacological blockade with Nimodipine.

claim: Thermosensation provokes Ca2+ influx in Class IV neurons.
source: Both these responses depended on two TRPA channels and the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel (L-VGCC), showing that the thermosensation provokes Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is inferred from the dependence on calcium channels and the observation of calcium transients.

claim: The precipitous fluctuation of firing rate in Class IV neurons enhanced the robust heat avoidance behavior.
source: The precipitous fluctuation of firing rate in Class IV neurons enhanced the robust heat avoidance.
evidence: This is demonstrated through optogenetic experiments showing that intermittent activation patterns increase rolling behavior.

claim: The Ca2+ influx can be a key signal encoding a specific modality in Class IV neurons.
source: We hypothesize that the Ca2+ influx can be a key signal encoding a specific modality.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the differential responses to thermal versus light stimuli.

claim: Mammalian C-fiber nociceptors detect harsh touch, high temperature, acid stimulus, and a number of toxic chemicals.
source: For example, mammalian C-fiber nociceptors detect harsh touch, high temperature, acid stimulus, and a number of toxic chemicals(Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Delmas et al., 2011; Perl, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels, PIEZO channels, and DEG/ENaC channels are the three protein superfamilies that form the molecular basis of thermal or mechanical nociceptive sensory transduction.
source: nowadays, molecular basis of thermal or mechanical nociceptive sensory transduction has primarily converged on three protein superfamilies: the TRP channels, the PIEZO channels, and the DEG/ENaC channels, all of which are well-conserved across many species (Basbaum et al., 2009; Geffeney and Goodman, 2012; Lumpkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRP channels are nonspecific cation channels.
source: TRP channels are nonspecific cation channels and several members of this family have been implicated in thermal nociception (Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Several members of the TRP channel family have been implicated in thermal nociception.
source: TRP channels are nonspecific cation channels and several members of this family have been implicated in thermal nociception (Lumpkin and Caterina, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: dTrpA1 is an essential component of both thermal and mechanical nociception in Drosophila.
source: For example, dTrpA1 is an essential component of both thermal and mechanical nociception in Drosophila (Zhong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PIEZO and DEG/ENaC channels are required specifically for mechanical nociception.
source: PIEZO and DEG/ENaC channels are required specifically for the mechanical nociception (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Coste et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The lite-1 gene in C. elegans encodes a light-activated G-protein-coupled receptor essential for noxious light sensation.
source: Both the lite-1 gene in C. elegans and Gustatory receptor 28b (Gr28b) gene in Drosophila encode the light-activated G-protein-coupled receptors and are essential for the noxious light sensation eliciting stereotypical light-avoidance behaviors (Liu et al., 2010; Xiang et al., 2010; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Gustatory receptor 28b (Gr28b) gene in Drosophila encodes a light-activated G-protein-coupled receptor essential for noxious light sensation.
source: Both the lite-1 gene in C. elegans and Gustatory receptor 28b (Gr28b) gene in Drosophila encode the light-activated G-protein-coupled receptors and are essential for the noxious light sensation eliciting stereotypical light-avoidance behaviors (Liu et al., 2010; Xiang et al., 2010; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C. elegans PVD neuron responds to harsh poke and cold temperatures.
source: the C. elegans PVD neuron responds to a harsh poke and cold temperatures (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: One subclass of multidendritic neurons in the Drosophila larva perceives a sharp poke, noxious high temperatures, and UV or blue light.
source: whereas one subclass of multidenritic neurons in the Drosophila larva perceives a sharp poke, noxious high temperatures, and UV or blue light (Im and Galko, 2012; Xiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila larvae exhibit distinct escape behavior outputs in response to thermal or mechanical stimuli versus blue light.
source: Intriguingly, Drosophila larvae exhibit distinct escape behavior outputs in response to the thermal or mechanical stimuli versus blue light (see below).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and referenced to be discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila dendritic arborization (da) neurons elaborate their dendritic arbors two-dimensionally on the basal surface of the epidermis.
source: Drosophila dendritic arborization (da) neurons constitute a subfamily of sensory neurons that elaborate their dendritic arbors two-dimensionally on the basal surface of the epidermis (Grueber et al., 2002; Han et al., 2012; Im and Galko, 2012; Jan and Jan, 2010; Kim et al., 2012a; Shimono et al., 2009; Yasunaga et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: da neurons in the larval abdominal hemisegment are classified into four morphological categories, Classes I-IV, in order of increasing territory size and/or branching complexity.
source: da neurons in the larval abdominal hemisegment are classified into four morphological categories, Classes I-IV, in order of increasing territory size and/or branching complexity (Grueber et al., 2002; Jan and Jan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Touching the dorsal cuticle of larvae with a metal probe hotter than 45°C evokes a stereotypic corkscrew-like escape rolling behavior.
source: Touching the dorsal cuticle of larvae with a metal probe hotter than 45°C evokes a stereotypic corkscrew-like escape rolling behavior (Babcock et al., 2009; Tracey et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of Class IV neurons is necessary and sufficient for the rolling behavior.
source: and activation of the Class IV neurons is necessary and sufficient for this output (Hwang et al., 2007; Ohyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thermal nociception behavior is mediated by thermoTRPs genes including Drosophila TRPA1 (dTrpA1), Painless, and Pyrexia.
source: This thermal nociception behavior is mediated by thermoTRPs genes including Drosophila TRPA1 (dTrpA1), Painless, and Pyrexia (Babcock et al., 2011; Hwang et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2005; Neely et al., 2010; 2011; Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strong mechanical stimuli, such as a sharp poke, elicit the same nocifensive behavior as noxious heat.
source: In addition to the noxious heat, strong mechanical stimuli, such as a sharp poke, elicit the same nocifensive behavior (Hwang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Class IV neurons are extra-ocular photoreceptors that respond to short-wavelength light stimuli and evoke a directional shift of locomotion, which requires Gr28b.
source: Moreover, Class IV neurons are extra-ocular photoreceptors that respond to short-wavelength light stimuli and evoke a directional shift of locomotion, which requires Gr28b (Berni et al., 2012; Xiang et al., 2010; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The IR laser allows quantitatively controlled step-like and local heating.
source: we built a new measurement system that combines three components: an infrared (IR) laser that allows quantitatively controlled step-like and local heating, neuronal calcium imaging, and extracellular single-unit recording to monitor firing patterns.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system developed in this study.

claim: The temperature within a radius of approximately 50 μm from the laser focus rapidly increased from an ambient temperature (25°C) to target temperatures (30–50°C) within 100 ms.
source: The temperature within a radius of approximately 50 μm from the laser focus rapidly increased from an ambient temperature (25°C) to target temperatures (30–50°C) within 100 ms, and stayed almost constant at the maximum temperature throughout the 1 s irradiation (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temperature measurements shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The temperature maximum was directly proportional to the power output of the laser.
source: Moreover, the temperature maximum was directly proportional to the power output of the laser (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through temperature measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IR-laser irradiation of more than 30-mW laser output power evoked high-frequency firings in Class IV neurons.
source: IR-laser irradiation of more than 30-mW laser output power evoked high-frequency firings in Class IV neurons (Figure 1D and E: 30 mW, 40.6 ± 4.8 Hz; 40 mW, 83.9 ± 7.3 Hz; n = 9 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: An irradiation of 1-mW raised the temperature by an increment of ~0.6°C in the focused region.
source: From our calibration of the IR laser, an irradiation of 1-mW raised the temperature by an increment of ~0.6°C in the focused region (inset of Figure 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through temperature calibration shown in Figure 1B inset.

claim: The estimated temperature was ~43°C for the 30-mW laser output power.
source: thus, the estimated temperature was ~43°C for the 30-mW laser output power.
evidence: This is calculated based on the calibration data.

claim: The threshold temperature for firing rate jumps was close to 40°C in previous experiments with perfusion of preheated solution.
source: This threshold temperature was close to that of previous experiments, where the jumps of the firing rate were detected at around 40°C with perfusion of the preheated solution into the recording chamber (Xiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature.

claim: dTrpA1 mutant and pain mutant exhibited normal basal firing in Class IV neurons.
source: dTrpA1 mutant (dTrpA11 homozygotes) and pain mutant (pain3 homozygotes) exhibited normal basal firing in the neurons (data not shown), but showed significantly lower firing rates during the IR-laser irradiation
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: dTrpA1 mutant and pain mutant showed significantly lower firing rates during IR-laser irradiation compared to wild-type.
source: dTrpA1 mutant (dTrpA11 homozygotes) and pain mutant (pain3 homozygotes) exhibited normal basal firing in the neurons (data not shown), but showed significantly lower firing rates during the IR-laser irradiation (Figure 1E: [dTrpA11] 30 mW: 0.5 ± 0.3 Hz, 40 mW: 43.8 ± 7.9 Hz, n = 10 cells; [pain3] 30 mW: 10.0 ± 3.0 Hz, 40 mW: 54.6 ± 4.8 Hz, n = 7 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1E.

claim: dTrpA11 mutants displayed significantly longer latency time between the onset of the IR irradiation and the increase in firing rate when compared to the wild-type or pain3 larvae.
source: Interestingly, dTrpA11 mutants displayed significantly longer latency time between the onset of the IR irradiation and the increase in firing rate when compared to the wild-type or pain3 larvae (Figure 1F and G; Time to Max. Firing Rate in Figure 1G: [wild type] 45.0 ± 7.1 ms, [dTrpA11] 698 ± 89.5 ms; [pain3] 61.6 ± 16.4 ms, p < 5.7×10-6, t-test with Bonferroni correction; our results of other allelic combinations are described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: The temporal pattern of the wild-type firing was not a simple summation of the two TRPA mutants.
source: The temporal pattern of the wild-type firing was not a simple summation of the two TRPA mutants; thus, we infer that the two heat-activated channels should function in a coordinated manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of firing patterns in mutants versus wild-type.

claim: The two heat-activated channels (dTrpA1 and Painless) function in a coordinated manner.
source: The temporal pattern of the wild-type firing was not a simple summation of the two TRPA mutants; thus, we infer that the two heat-activated channels should function in a coordinated manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of firing patterns in mutants versus wild-type.

claim: The firing responses of the wild-type neurons reflected intrinsic neuronal activities, dependent on the heat-activated channels and were not induced by photo damage.
source: Our results also strongly suggested that the firing responses of the wild-type neurons reflected intrinsic neuronal activities, dependent on the heat-activated channels and were not induced by photo damage (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic experiments and control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the soma was irradiated with the IR laser, a large increase in Ca2+ was observed over the entire dendritic tree.
source: When the soma was irradiated with the IR laser, a large increase in Ca2+ was observed over the entire dendritic tree, which we designated as dendritic Ca2+ transients or simply Ca2+ transients (Figure 2A,B and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging shown in Figure 2A, B and Video 1.

claim: The rise of the Ca2+ transients emerged simultaneously in both proximal and distal dendrites.
source: The rise of the Ca2+ transients emerged simultaneously in both proximal and distal dendrites, and decayed exponentially.
evidence: This is an observation from the calcium imaging data.

claim: The Ca2+ transients occurred in all-or-none fashion upon IR-laser irradiations.
source: The Ca2+ transients occurred in all-or-none fashion upon IR-laser irradiations; suggesting that the magnitude of the thermal stimuli was converted into another value of information (e.g. dendritic membrane potential), and the value higher than a presumptive threshold evoked Ca2+ transients.
evidence: This is an observation from the calcium imaging data.

claim: The probabilities of the occurrence of Ca2+ transients were dependent on the output powers of the IR-laser.
source: The probabilities of the occurrence of Ca2+ transients were dependent on the output powers of the IR-laser, which arose abruptly at around 36 mW (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The probabilities of Ca2+ transients were significantly lowered in the neurons of dTrpA1 or pain mutants.
source: Furthermore, the probabilities were significantly lowered in the neurons of dTrpA1 or pain mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that Ca2+ transients also reflect normal neuronal activities that depend on the heat-activated channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data in mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Ca2+ transients reflect normal neuronal activities that depend on the heat-activated channels.
source: Furthermore, the probabilities were significantly lowered in the neurons of dTrpA1 or pain mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that Ca2+ transients also reflect normal neuronal activities that depend on the heat-activated channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments showing reduced Ca2+ transients in mutants.

claim: Irradiation to the dendritic arbor also evoked Ca2+ transients, although this required higher IR-laser power compared to the stimulation of the soma.
source: Irradiation to the dendritic arbor also evoked Ca2+ transients, although this required higher IR-laser power compared to the stimulation of the soma (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Excitability of Class IV neurons was prerequisite for the Ca2+ transient.
source: Excitability of Class IV neurons was prerequisite for this Ca2+ transient, as shown by the fact that the occurrence of the transients was completely blocked by overexpression of the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 (Figure 2D), which hyperpolarizes neurons and decreases their resting membrane potential (Hardie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic manipulation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Overexpression of the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 completely blocked the occurrence of Ca2+ transients.
source: Excitability of Class IV neurons was prerequisite for this Ca2+ transient, as shown by the fact that the occurrence of the transients was completely blocked by overexpression of the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 (Figure 2D), which hyperpolarizes neurons and decreases their resting membrane potential (Hardie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic manipulation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Kir2.1 hyperpolarizes neurons and decreases their resting membrane potential.
source: which hyperpolarizes neurons and decreases their resting membrane potential (Hardie et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Normal Ca2+ transients hardly occurred in L-type VGCC mutants (Ca-α1DX7/AR66 and Ca-α1DX10/AR66).
source: A dramatic phenotype was found in mutants of the L-type VGCC gene (Ca-α1DX7/AR66 and Ca-α1DX10/AR66)(Eberl et al., 1998); normal Ca2+ transients hardly occurred in those mutants (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calcium imaging data in mutants shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: A selective inhibitor of L-type VGCC, Nimodipine, caused a similar defect in Ca2+ transients as the L-type VGCC mutants.
source: A similar defect was observed in the wild type when a selective inhibitor of L-type VGCC, Nimodipine (Gielow et al., 1995; Grey and Burrell, 2010), was applied (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: L-type VGCC-mediated excitability is required for the occurrence of Ca2+ transients in Class IV neurons.
source: These results showed that L-type VGCC-mediated excitability is required for the occurrence of Ca2+ transients in Class IV neurons
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and pharmacological experiments.

claim: The addition of Tetrodotoxin (TTX) had no effect on the dendritic Ca2+ transients in Class IV neurons.
source: In our system, however, the addition of Tetrodotoxin (TTX) had no effect on the dendritic Ca2+ transients in Class IV neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and E), indicating that VGSCs are required neither for the occurrence of Ca2+ transients nor for the regenerative propagation of membrane potential along the dendritic branches.
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and E.

claim: VGSCs are required neither for the occurrence of Ca2+ transients nor for the regenerative propagation of membrane potential along the dendritic branches.
source: In our system, however, the addition of Tetrodotoxin (TTX) had no effect on the dendritic Ca2+ transients in Class IV neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and E), indicating that VGSCs are required neither for the occurrence of Ca2+ transients nor for the regenerative propagation of membrane potential along the dendritic branches.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of TTX on Ca2+ transients.

claim: Peak amplitudes of Ca2+ transients did not display a strong correlation with maximum firing rates under 40-mW IR-laser irradiation.
source: Under 40-mW IR-laser irradiation, peak amplitudes of Ca2+ transients did not display a strong correlation with maximum firing rates (Figure 3B; p > 0.46, ρ = 0.17, Spearman's rank correlation test; n = 20 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simultaneous calcium imaging and electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The occurrence of US showed a high correlation with the peak amplitude of Ca2+ transients.
source: When we sorted datasets of the firing patterns in a descending order of the peak amplitude of Ca2+ transients, the occurrence of US showed a high correlation with the peak amplitude (Figure 3D and E; p < 1.9×10–8, ρ = 0.91; Spearman's rank correlation test; n = 20 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simultaneous calcium imaging and electrophysiology shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: In each dataset, the minimal interspike interval within the US was invariably shorter than that within non-US firings.
source: More importantly, in each dataset, the minimal interspike interval within the US was invariably shorter than that within non-US firings (Figure 3F; p < 5.2×10–6; paired Student's t-test; n = 13 cells), indicating that large excitatory currents existed just prior to the pause in firing
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of interspike intervals shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Large excitatory currents existed just prior to the pause in firing.
source: More importantly, in each dataset, the minimal interspike interval within the US was invariably shorter than that within non-US firings (Figure 3F; p < 5.2×10–6; paired Student's t-test; n = 13 cells), indicating that large excitatory currents existed just prior to the pause in firing
evidence: This is inferred from the shorter interspike intervals within US.

claim: Ca2+ transients and US were hardly detected in the spike trains in the presence of Nimodipine.
source: To address how inhibition of L-type VGCC affects the firing rate and the occurrence of Ca2+ transients and US, we recorded Class IV neurons in the presence of Nimodipine. Ca2+ transients and US were hardly detected in the spike trains (Figure 3G,H, and J; [Control] 1.6 ± 0.32, [Nimodipine] 0 ± 0; p = 0.001, Wilcoxon's rank-sum test; n = 20 cells [Control] and n = 11 cells [Nimodipine])
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3G, H, and J.

claim: The firing rate was not decreased compared to that of the control and showed its peak around 100 Hz in the presence of Nimodipine.
source: in contrast, the firing rate was not decreased compared to that of the control and showed its peak around 100 Hz (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The L-type VGCC is essential for the generation of US.
source: In other words, firing patterns were modified as if the 'burst and pause' pattern had been replaced with conventional high-frequency spike trains, indicating that the L-type VGCC is essential for the generation of US.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological experiments with Nimodipine.

claim: Dendritic Ca2+ transients observed in response to heat produced by the IR laser are generated by accumulations of L-type VGCC-dependent Ca2+ spikes in Class IV neurons.
source: Collectively, our findings strongly suggest that dendritic Ca2+ transients we observed in response to heat produced by the IR laser are generated by accumulations of L-type VGCC-dependent Ca2+ spikes in Class IV neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined evidence from calcium imaging and electrophysiology.

claim: TrpA1-A-expressing neurons evoke both Ca2+ transients and the unique firing pattern below 20 mW.
source: Consistent with this speculation, our recordings demonstrated that TrpA1-A-expressing neurons (TrpA1-A+ neurons) evoke both Ca2+ transients and the unique firing pattern below 20 mW (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), to which the wild-type neurons were insensitive (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with ectopic expression of dTrpA1-A shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Spikes detected in somata by extracellular single-unit recordings propagate faithfully through their axons.
source: Nonetheless, our findings indicate that the spikes recorded extracellularly from Class IV soma propagate faithfully through its axon (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D, see also the legends).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dual extracellular recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: Both the occurrence of the Ca2+ transient and that of the unique firing pattern were suppressed in Ca-α1D-knockdown Class IV neurons.
source: We first examined the physiological responses of Ca-α1D-knockdown Class IV neurons. Both the occurrence of the Ca2+ transient and that of the unique firing pattern were suppressed in the neurons (Figure 4A and B) without a dramatic decrease in firing rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with RNAi knockdown shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The total US number was significantly decreased in Ca-α1D-knockdown neurons compared to controls.
source: We also observed that the total US number was significantly decreased in Ca-α1D-knockdown neurons compared to controls (Figure 4C; [white RNAi GL00094] 1.55 ± 0.20 total US number, [Ca-α1D RNAi HMS00294] 1.00 ± 0.00; p = 0.0055; Wilcoxon's rank-sum test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with RNAi knockdown shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ca-α1D mutant larvae displayed a significantly delayed response to the heat probe.
source: We then examined how Ca-α1D mutant larvae (Ca-α1DX10/AR66) responded to the heat probe and found that they displayed a significantly delayed response (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is impaired in the Ca-α1D mutant larvae.
source: However it was reported that synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is impaired in the Ca-α1D mutant larvae due to abrogation of the Ca2+ influx in both muscles and motor neurons (Ren et al., 1998; Worrell and Levine, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The knockdown larvae displayed significantly delayed response in the rolling behavior than the control larvae.
source: Therefore, we knocked down expression of L-type VGCC selectively in Class IV neurons as was previously done (Kanamori et al., 2013). The phenotypic defect of the knockdown larvae was less dramatic than that of the whole-body mutant; nonetheless, the knockdown larvae displayed significantly delayed response in the rolling behavior than the control larvae (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments with RNAi knockdown shown in Figure 4F.

claim: L-type VGCC-dependent unique firing patterns in Class IV neurons are necessary for the highly penetrant induction of the larval nocifensive rolling behavior.
source: These data support our hypothesis that L-type VGCC-dependent unique firing patterns in Class IV neurons are necessary for the highly penetrant induction of the larval nocifensive rolling behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral and physiological experiments.

claim: Ca-α1D-knockdown larvae displayed rolling when the continuous firing pattern was evoked, and the rolling occurred more efficiently by the pulsatile optogenetic activation.
source: In live animals, Ca-α1D-knockdown larvae displayed rolling when the continuous firing pattern was evoked, and the rolling occurred more efficiently by the pulsatile optogenetic activation (Figure 5B; [Continuous] 65.3 ± 9.2%, n = 75, [Intermittent] 86.3 ± 5.9%, n = 95, mean ± 95% confidence interval based on Clopper-Pearson method; p = 0.0017, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 'total peak number' showed a significant correlation with the total US number in control neurons.
source: With this analysis, the 'total peak number' showed a significant correlation with the total US number in control neurons (p = 3.17 x 10–5, ρ = 0.79; Spearman's rank correlation test; n = 20 cells; Figure 3K).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of firing patterns shown in Figure 3K.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the total peak number in Nimodipine-applied neurons.
source: We then showed a significant decrease in the total peak number in Nimodipine-applied neurons (Figure 3L; [Control] 2.00 ± 0.21 total peak number, [Nimodipine] 1.09 ± 0.091; p = 0.0034; Wilcoxon's rank-sum test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The total peak number was significantly decreased in Ca-α1D-knockdown neurons compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, the total peak number was significantly decreased in Ca-α1D-knockdown neurons compared to controls (Figure 4D; [white RNAi GL00094] 1.55 ± 0.20 total peak number, [Ca-α1D RNAi HMS00294] 1.00 ± 0.00; p = 0.027).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with RNAi knockdown shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The total peak number of firing rate fluctuation in Class IV neurons plays a key role in increasing the likelihood of rolling locomotion upon noxious heat input.
source: These results suggest that the total number of peaks of firing rate fluctuation in Class IV neurons plays a key role in increasing the likelihood of rolling locomotion upon noxious heat input.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined evidence from optogenetics, pharmacology, and genetics.

claim: Ca-α1D-knockdown larvae avoided blue light, as did the control larvae.
source: Ca-α1D-knockdown larvae avoided blue light, as did the control larvae, when they were illuminated (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: L-type VGCC is dispensable for the photo-avoidance behavior.
source: This finding indicates that not only L-type VGCC is dispensable for the photo-avoidance behavior, but also the synaptic transmission at the NMJ is not severely affected under our Ca-α1D knockdown condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal photo-avoidance behavior in Ca-α1D-knockdown larvae.

claim: 'US-like spikes' were detected only under the strongest light condition.
source: (2) 'US-like spikes' (compare its definition in the inset of Figure 6E with that of US in Figure 3C) were detected only under the strongest light condition (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings with blue light stimulation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ca2+ transients were not observed at a light intensity of 146.7 mW/mm2.
source: (3) Ca2+ transients were not observed at a light intensity (146.7 mW/mm2; data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The wild-type Class IV did not generate L-type VGCC-dependent US in response to the blue light.
